source_text: Primae igitur definitionis eversu culmina eius in solum cuneus rationis effudit. Quid igitur de te speras, cuius tria sunt ita in lubrico sicut illius unum? Dicis enim primo naturale esse peccatum, secundo bonum Deum, qui mala id est peccata condat informet extendat, tertio vero rem voluntatis immixtam esse seminibus. Haec ergo tria definitionum tuarum capita singula apud semet vacillant; vacillant, inquio, immo ut funes e sabulo dilabuntur, ante quam coeant. Unum ergo id est naturale peccatum iam in Manichaeo ex directo quidem destructum iacet; alia autem duo quae opinionis vestrae sunt propria, Manichaeo totidem intereunte sed consueta ceciderunt. Nam si ille reos nasci homines nec per malam naturam nec per principem tenebrarum potuit vindicare, quanto magis vos stulti, qui ad ostendenda nascentium crimina iunxistis accusationem Dei? Ac per hoc, sicut non potest natura esse peccatum, quo fulmine Manichaei dogma dissiluit, ita recurrit, ut, quod peccatum est, naturale esse non possit; res enim voluntatis non transit in conditionem substantiae, quod tu factum arbitraris. Multo autem magis constat Deum bonum malos numquam creare, apparuit itaque peccatum in nascente, quem Deus creat, esse non posse.
pass_a_gloss: By the overthrow therefore of the first definition the wedge of reason has poured his rooftops onto the ground. What therefore do you hope of yourself, whose three are so on the slippery as that one's one? For you say first that sin is natural, second a good God who founds, forms, extends evils, that is sins, third truly that a thing of will has been mixed into seeds. These three heads therefore of your definitions each vacillate at themselves; they vacillate, I say, nay as ropes they slide from sand before they come together. One therefore, that is natural sin, already lies destroyed in the Manichaean from the direct; but the other two which are proper of your opinion have fallen with the Manichaean perishing equally but customarily. For if he could not vindicate humans born defendants either through an evil nature or through the prince of darkness, how much more you foolish, who to show the crimes of those being born have joined the accusation of God? And through this, as nature cannot be sin, by which thunderbolt the dogma of the Manichaean burst apart, so it runs back that what is sin cannot be natural; for a thing of will does not pass into the condition of a substance, which you judge has been done. But much more it stands that a good God never creates evils; it has appeared therefore that sin cannot be in one being born whom God creates.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: By overthrowing his first definition, the wedge of reason brought his rooftops crashing to the ground. What hope have you, then, whose three claims stand on ground as slippery as his one? First you say sin is natural. Second, that God is good although he creates, shapes, and extends evils—that is, sins. Third, that an act of will has been mixed into reproductive seed. Each of these three heads of your definitions totters in itself. Totters, I say? Rather, like ropes made of sand, they fall apart before coming together.

One claim—natural sin—already lies destroyed in the direct defeat of Mani. The other two, peculiar to your opinion, fell in the same familiar destruction that struck him. If he could not establish that humans are born guilty through either an evil nature or the prince of darkness, how much more foolish are you, who added an accusation against God to demonstrate newborn children’s crimes! Just as nature cannot be sin—the thunderbolt that shattered Mani’s doctrine—so, conversely, what is sin cannot be natural. An act of will does not pass into the condition of a substance, as you suppose happened. Much more certainly, the good God never creates evil beings. Thus it has become clear that sin cannot exist in a newborn whom God creates.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
